Town
toun
n. (a settlement smaller than a city, often unwalled; rendering Hebrew ir, Greek kome)
Old English tūn, an enclosure, a farmstead; the word grew from the fence to what the fence held. The Greek kome is a village as against a walled city.

Biblical Definition

Rahab's house “was upon the town wall” (Jos 2:15). “The elders of the town trembled” at Samuel's coming to Bethlehem (1Sa 16:4). Christ sent the twelve “into whatsoever city or town ye shall enter” (Mat 10:11), led the blind man of Bethsaida “out of the town” and told him afterward, “Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town” (Mar 8:23, 26). Bethlehem is “the town where David was” (John 7:42), and Bethany “the town of Mary and her sister Martha” (John 11:1). Habakkuk pronounces “Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity!” (Hab 2:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines town as any collection of houses larger than a village; in the Scriptures, a walled or fenced place.

expand to see more

TOWN, n. Originally, a walled or fortified place; a collection of houses inclosed with walls, hedges or palisades.

2. Any collection of houses, larger than a village.

3. In the United States, the whole territory within certain limits, a township.

Key Scripture

Mat 10:11 — "And into whatsoever city or town ye shall enter, enquire who in it is worthy; and there abide till ye go thence."

Mar 8:26 — "And he sent him away to his house, saying, Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town."

John 7:42 — "Hath not the scripture said, That Christ cometh of the seed of David, and out of the town of Bethlehem, where David was?"

John 11:1 — "Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany, the town of Mary and her sister Martha."

Hab 2:12 — "Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity!"

Modern Corruption

Christ's silence to the man of Bethsaida is read as false modesty, when Bethsaida was a town He had already pronounced woe upon.

expand to see more

The blind man of Mark 8 is led out of the town before he is healed and told not to go back into it after, and the reader assumes the Lord is being shy about miracles. He had already said of that town, “Woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago” (Mat 11:21). A town that has seen the works and not repented is not given more works to ignore. Judgment in the Gospels is often quiet: the Lord simply stops performing for the people who will not believe, and the healed man is sent home by another road.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ir (H5892), a city, town; Greek kome (G2968), a village, unwalled town; komopolis (G2969), a town.

expand to see more

Hebrew ir (H5892) — city, town; 1 Samuel 16:4, Habakkuk 2:12, Joshua 2:15.

Greek kome (G2968) — village, town; Matthew 10:11, Mark 8:23, 8:26, John 7:42, 11:1, 11:30.

Greek komopolis (G2969) — a country town; Mark 1:38 only.

Usage

"“Into whatsoever city or town ye shall enter” — the twelve sent out."

"“Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town” — Bethsaida cut off from further signs."

"“Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood” — Habakkuk on the Chaldean."
